title: Bewitched sleep: Russians’ views on Ukraine and the world – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Drawing on 14 Levada-Center focus groups (April-August 2026) and polls, ECFR finds Russians treat the Ukraine war as an unchangeable, inconvenient reality, expect it to last years, and sink into a passive 'bewitched sleep' that poses no near-term threat to the Kremlin despite inflation and petrol shortages. Europe has replaced the US as enemy-in-chief, China is seen as a self-interested ally of necessity, and the authors urge Europe to fund exile media, universities and grassroots contact because 'something is off' and a sudden shift cannot be ruled out.

insights.claim: Russians treat the Ukraine war as a given they cannot change: most assume Russia will prevail through size and power, but nobody regards it as existential or noble, and all groups unanimously said victory would not be more important than victory in the second world war.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: Low emotional investment means the Kremlin faces neither pressure to end the war nor a mobilised nationalist base demanding escalation.
insights.quote: Russians treat the war as a given; a reality they cannot change
insights.locator: Overall, across the groups it is clear

insights.claim: Focus group participants overwhelmingly expect the war to last another two to three years, some into the 2030s, and several groups assume it will become a 'forever war' like the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: Russian public opinion offers no catalyst for a near-term ceasefire; markets should not price an imminent end to the war or sanctions relief from domestic pressure.
insights.quote: The end of the war is not close. Maybe in the 2030s.
insights.locator: The war

insights.claim: Russians cannot articulate the war's aims or what victory looks like, which leaves the Kremlin free to define 'victory' however it wishes — one participant said 'We will accept anything the higher-ups define as victory'.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: Putin has wide domestic latitude to accept or reject any settlement, so negotiation outcomes depend on Kremlin calculus, not public opinion.
insights.quote: We will accept anything the higher-ups define as victory
insights.locator: With the aims of the war poorly understood

insights.claim: The 2022 explanation that Russia started the war to defend Donetsk and Luhansk has all but vanished, replaced by a defensive narrative that 'if Russia had not hit first, they would have attacked'.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: Shifting justifications show propaganda adapting to a preventive-war frame, which can justify an indefinite conflict.
insights.locator: When asked why the war began

insights.claim: Polls show 61% of Russians think it is time for peace negotiations, yet 59% say that if peace cannot be achieved Russia should intensify attacks rather than offer concessions to Ukraine; most agree peace must be on Russia's terms.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: Desire for peace does not translate into support for compromise, limiting room for a negotiated settlement with Ukrainian concessions from Russia.
insights.quote: the majority (61%) of Russians think it is time for peace negotiations
insights.locator: Things in Russia are static

insights.claim: Most Russians do not see Ukraine as fully sovereign, which makes the war more palatable: if the adversary is not a 'proper country', this is not a 'proper war', lowering the temperature and numbing people to its suffering.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: Denial of Ukrainian statehood underpins public tolerance of maximalist war aims.
insights.quote: a proper war could happen against a proper country; if the adversary is not a proper country, then that is not a proper war
insights.locator: The views aired suggest that the war

insights.claim: Russians are sceptical the war will widen to attacks on other neighbours or a NATO-Russia conflict, and there is no demand for broader escalation, e.g. against the Baltic states.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: Absence of public appetite for escalation is a modest constraint, though respondents admit they cannot predict Kremlin decisions.
insights.quote: We will not go there, I do not understand why we would, we are not idiots
insights.locator: When asked whether the war could go beyond

themes.theme: Economic and social costs inside Russia

insights.claim: Ukraine's deep drone strikes are causing petrol shortages and visible blasts at Russian warehouses, increasing anxiety in spring-summer 2026 but not producing panic or any readiness to confront the Kremlin.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: Ukraine's strike campaign on Russian energy infrastructure is felt domestically (fuel shortages) but has not created political pressure.
insights.quote: the resulting petrol shortages and videos of blasts at Russia’s warehouses certainly do
insights.locator: The conversations take place from late spring

insights.claim: Inflation and the cost of living — especially young people's inability to afford apartments — are the dominant complaints, but Russians do not blame the war for these problems and respond by working more and spending less.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: Economic pain from war spending is real but politically inert, so sanctions-induced inflation is unlikely to force a policy change by itself.
insights.quote: What everyone feels and complains about is inflation.
insights.locator: What everyone feels and complains about

insights.claim: Participants expect Ukraine reconstruction in Russian-controlled areas to be funded from Russia's budget at the expense of domestic social spending, note health funding is already falling, and many expect sanctions and pariah status to persist for years even after the war.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: Implies continued fiscal strain and crowding-out of social spending in Russia, and limited expectation of post-war normalisation.
insights.quote: I can see that financing of social sphere, including health care, is decreasing
insights.locator: The cost

insights.claim: People fear the Kremlin may take unpopular steps such as intensified mobilisation after the September Duma election; men mostly say they would not volunteer but many would comply with mobilisation as a duty.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: A post-election mobilisation wave would be a signal of escalation and could hit Russian labour markets further.
insights.locator: There is also a sense that things could get worse

insights.claim: Russians dread the return of war veterans, fearing domestic violence, and compare them to Afghan war veterans associated with criminality — contradicting Kremlin propaganda that hails them as a new patriotic elite.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: Demobilisation could bring social instability and crime, a latent post-war risk for the regime.
insights.quote: people dread the return of veterans, fearing new violence at home
insights.locator: Veterans

themes.theme: Russia's view of friends: China and the failed 'turn to Eurasia'

insights.claim: Russians see China as a self-interested ally of necessity whose deals are skewed in its favour, treating Russia as a raw-materials source, and which benefits most while Russia and the West weaken each other over Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: Public scepticism of China signals the Sino-Russian partnership is asymmetric, with Beijing capturing terms of trade on Russian commodities.
insights.quote: They buy timber from us and then sell us furniture made of sawdust
insights.locator: As for China, the relationship clearly has its limits

insights.claim: Russians think Xi Jinping would beat Putin at chess while Putin would beat Trump, reflecting a belief that China is smarter and better at long-term strategy.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: Perceived Chinese strategic superiority hints at latent Russian unease over junior-partner status.
insights.locator: Many also think China is smarter than Russia

insights.claim: Putin's 'turn to Eurasia', policy since 2012, has gained no traction with the public: few think Russia's destiny lies in Asia, and some say 'If we survive, we will most likely be Europe'.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: Underlying European cultural identification suggests a potential post-Putin re-engagement with Europe.
insights.quote: If we survive, we will most likely be Europe
insights.locator: The “turn to Eurasia”

insights.claim: Russians are well informed about foreign shifts, commonly noting 'Hungary used to be an ally, but no more', with China and Belarus at the top of their friends list and Belarus seen as a dependent with no choice.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: Russian public tracks European political changes closely, so shifts in EU unity are visible inside Russia.
insights.quote: Hungary used to be an ally, but no more
insights.locator: All groups were asked which countries

insights.claim: The Trump presidency shifted the US from Russia's arch-enemy role it held for most of this century — high hopes that Trump would end the war faded but US status did not revert — and Europe now occupies the role of enemy-in-chief.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: A US-Russia thaw at the popular level alongside Europe's demonisation supports the risk of US-Russia bilateral deals that sideline Europe.
insights.quote: Now Europe occupies the role of the enemy-in-chief.
insights.locator: Remarkably, the Trump presidency has shifted

insights.claim: Polls show Russian attitudes towards Europe are worse than towards America and almost on a par with views of Ukraine, with Britain, France and Germany named first among enemies, followed by the Baltic states, Finland and Poland.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: Hostility concentrates on Europe's major powers and frontline states — consistent with these being targets of Russian hybrid pressure.
insights.locator: If the list of Russia’s allies is quite short

insights.claim: Almost no Russian connects European antagonism or sanctions to Russia's own invasion of Ukraine; a Moscow sociologist notes Russia's own role tends to be forgotten so sanctions are perceived as unprovoked Western attacks.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: Sanctions are unlikely to shift Russian public opinion against the war since they are read as Western aggression.
insights.quote: On what basis is the US even imposing sanctions on us?!
insights.locator: This brings to mind a conversation

insights.claim: Russians nonetheless expect relations with Europe to improve sooner than with the US — likely only after Putin leaves — and on a pragmatic, commercial basis ('business logic will prevail'), not with Europe as a role model.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: Post-Putin Russia may seek resumed commodity trade with Europe, relevant to long-term energy and trade scenarios.
insights.quote: They’ll again start buying things from us … business logic will prevail.
insights.locator: But, when it comes to the future

themes.theme: 'Bewitched sleep' and the potential for sudden change

insights.claim: Russians sink, often voluntarily, into a 'bewitched sleep' of withdrawal into family survival, explained less by fear of repression than by a sense of lacking agency; this is reflected in Putin's approval rating never dropping below 59%.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: Regime stability rests on mass political passivity rather than enthusiasm — stable now but potentially brittle.
insights.quote: Putin’s own approval rating, which has never dropped below 59%
insights.locator: This is not explicable solely by fear

insights.claim: Kremlin narratives succeed not because they are imposed but because they resonate with existing public biases; a Moscow scholar says society ceased to see itself as a political actor and there is no reason to expect change soon.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: No near-term protest risk: economic and logistical problems are unlikely to produce a movement constraining the regime.
insights.quote: Society ceased to perceive itself as a political actor a while ago—one of the achievements of Putin’s regime.
insights.locator: Furthermore, the regime’s justifications

insights.claim: Despite static surface opinion, sociologists and participants sense 'something is off' and 'soon something will blow up'; possible triggers include the worsening economy, elite anxiety, lack of battlefield results or leadership change, though timing is unknowable.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: Tail risk of abrupt political discontinuity in Russia, as with the unpredicted Soviet collapse, should not be ignored in scenario planning.
insights.quote: Something is ‘off’. We can’t pinpoint what exactly it is, but something is indeed off.
insights.locator: Yet it is not impossible that social

insights.claim: In most focus groups at least one participant held pronounced anti-war views, and in one group they formed a majority; these 'non-sleepers' feel isolated and frequently drew barbed wire, graveyards and concentration camps when asked to depict the future.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: A small, isolated anti-war minority exists that Western outreach could support.
insights.locator: However, some Russians refuse to slip

themes.theme: How Europe should reach Russian society

insights.claim: With the US having folded USAID programming for Russian civil society and media and preferring direct engagement with the Kremlin, Europeans may need to fund a bigger share of Russian-language independent media, exile universities and exiled cultural figures.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: Funding responsibility for Russian information-space operations is shifting to EU budgets.
insights.locator: Reduced American funding for democracy

insights.claim: Labelling all Russians as aggressors reinforces biases and serves regime propaganda; Western language should instead centre on universal values and support initiatives such as Memorial, boosting the anti-war minority's morale.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: Blanket collective punishment policies (e.g. visa bans) may be counterproductive for Europe's long-term aims.
insights.locator: Convey shared values instead of blanket generalisations

insights.claim: European approaches to Russian exiles should be coordinated but not uniform given different threat exposure: Estonia plans for possible land invasion and stripped resident Russians of local voting rights, France and Italy face mainly cyber and information operations, and Poland, Romania and Germany have experienced sabotage and drone incursions.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: Threat exposure varies sharply within the EU, with frontline states facing kinetic and sabotage risk.
insights.locator: While coordinating European approaches

insights.claim: Russians with personal experience of the West hold views that are, without exception, more positive and reality-based than those formed from state television, showing that grassroots contact works and should be governed deliberately rather than left to chance or the Kremlin.
insights.speaker: Jana Kobzová, Kadri Liik
insights.so_what: Argues against total people-to-people isolation of Russia as part of European sanctions policy.
insights.quote: Grassroots communication and interaction—people meeting and talking with others—really works.
insights.locator: Deliberate hope
